topic: Virtual Inheritance and the Implementation of Virtual Base Classes
explanation:
Virtual inheritance in C++ addresses the "diamond problem"—where multiple inheritance leads to ambiguous base class subobjects.  The compiler implements this using a technique involving a shared virtual base class subobject. This avoids redundant copies of the virtual base and ensures a single instance of the base class's data members.  Instead of directly embedding the virtual base, the compiler creates a pointer (or a pointer-sized offset) to the shared virtual base within the derived class's object layout.  This pointer is typically set during construction.  The actual data members of the virtual base class reside in a separate memory location shared among all classes inheriting virtually from it.  Accessing members of the virtual base class involves indirect access via this pointer, incurring a slight performance overhead compared to non-virtual inheritance. This overhead is generally small and far outweighed by the benefits of avoiding ambiguity.

Different compilers may employ various optimization strategies.  Some compilers might apply pointer-swizzling (modifying the vptr of derived classes to directly point to the shared virtual base's vtable) to reduce the cost of virtual base access for certain access patterns.

The memory layout is considerably more complex than single or non-virtual multiple inheritance.  Consider the size and alignment requirements of each base class as well as potential padding added for alignment constraints. The compiler must meticulously manage memory offsets to ensure correct access to members of all base classes including the virtual base.

Cross-platform differences in pointer size and alignment rules will also influence the layout and the efficiency of pointer arithmetic used to navigate the object memory.
